title: Good Behaviour Is Not Defined Explicitly
summary: This failure occurs when domain knowledge about correct, useful, or trustworthy product behaviour exists in the team but remains tacit. The practical issue is not absence of expertise; it is the absence of an explicit design artefact that the interface enforces, communicates, or exposes to users.
keyFacts: The failure concerns tacit knowledge that exists in experienced team members but is not encoded in the product interface.
It differs from having no clear behaviour model: in this failure, the team can describe good behaviour, but has not turned that knowledge into an explicit design artefact.
One expression is an interface that cannot represent the full reasoning domain experts bring to the work.
A second expression, common in AI-assisted products, is surfacing AI outputs without surfacing the criteria users need to evaluate those outputs.
In the Callsign case, fraud analysts' strategy knowledge exceeded what the pre-redesign rule interface could represent.
In the Puraite case, four iterations of the AI suggestion display converted implicit systematic-review evaluation knowledge into an explicit interface specification.
KISPE Space used 61 behavioural rules in ten families to make tacit expectations explicit as checkable design requirements before build.

Schone Airspace Group used 12 principal interaction contracts, eight operational invariants, and eight non-negotiable interface rules to specify intended interface behaviour from design and integration perspectives.
Client-reported outcomes in the Callsign and Puraite examples are not field-measured task-time, error-rate, or independent performance data.

bodySections.heading: Summary
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Good behaviour is not defined explicitly when a team knows what correct or high-quality product behaviour looks like, but that knowledge remains tacit. Experienced members can describe the difference between a good output and a weak output, but the interface does not encode, expose, or enforce the criteria behind that judgement.

This is a design failure rather than a training failure. The knowledge exists in the team. The missing work is converting that knowledge into explicit interface requirements, interaction structures, evaluation criteria, or checkable behaviour specifications.

bodySections.heading: Tacit Judgement Is Not Converted Into Interface Requirements
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Good behaviour is not defined explicitly when experienced people carry the product's real quality standard in their heads, in code review comments, in onboarding, or in accumulated institutional knowledge. The product does not carry that standard. Users who do not already possess the same experience cannot reliably apply it.

In complex products, this gap can affect what the system does and how users judge what the system produces. A fraud analyst may know which behavioural-signal combinations indicate a specific fraud pattern. A systematic reviewer may know which publication evidence supports an inclusion or exclusion decision. A clinical protocol implementer may know which query structure correctly represents the protocol. If the interface does not make this knowledge explicit, the product behaves or presents outputs without giving users the full standard needed to configure, interpret, or challenge it.

The consequence is that the product operates at the level of the interface's expressive capacity, not at the level of the domain knowledge available in the organisation. Knowledge that cannot be represented in the interface cannot govern the product's behaviour through normal use.

bodySections.heading: How This Differs From Having No Clear Behaviour Model
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Good behaviour not being defined explicitly is adjacent to the product has no clear behaviour model, but the starting condition is different. A product with no clear behaviour model has no specified answer to what the system should do under a given condition. The team cannot answer the behaviour question cleanly, even implicitly.

Good behaviour not being defined explicitly is a different condition. The team can answer the behaviour question in conversation. Experienced members can describe what good behaviour looks like. The failure is that the answer has not been converted into a design artefact that the interface embodies.

The practical distinction matters. A team with no behaviour model needs to discover and specify what good behaviour should be. A team with implicit but unencoded knowledge needs to surface, structure, and codify what experienced members already know.

bodySections.heading: Domain Expertise That the Interface Cannot Represent
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
One expression of this failure is an interface that cannot represent the reasoning that domain experts use in the work. The expert may be able to articulate the required behaviour, but the interaction architecture cannot carry it.

In a fraud-detection policy engine, a simple rule interface may express if condition X, then action Y. That structure may be insufficient for fraud strategy that depends on combinations of signals, conditional exceptions, customer segments, sequencing logic, and auditability. When those structures are not representable in the interface, expert knowledge can only enter the product through engineering intervention or through simplified approximations.

This is not a failure of the expert to articulate knowledge. It is a failure of the product design to provide enough expressive depth for the domain. The product's behaviour becomes governed by the subset of expertise that the interface can represent.

bodySections.heading: AI Outputs Without Visible Evaluation Criteria
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A second expression appears in AI-assisted products when the interface displays AI outputs without displaying the criteria users need to evaluate those outputs. The output is visible, but the standard for judging the output is absent.

Experienced users may compensate with their own domain knowledge. They may recognise when an AI inclusion decision is grounded in the relevant publication text, when a fraud flag is well founded, or when a suggested action is weak. Less experienced users cannot make the same judgement reliably if the interface does not provide the evidence and criteria at the point of decision.

This matters for capability democratisation. A product that only works for users who already bring the evaluation criteria does not broaden access to expert capability. It shifts work to the user's private judgement instead of making the judgement criteria part of the interface.

bodySections.heading: Callsign Fraud Authentication: Fraud Strategy Knowledge Was Not Representable in the Interface
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the documented Callsign fraud authentication case, the policy engine was intended to let fraud analysts encode strategies that governed real-time authentication decisions. The analysts had specific knowledge about behavioural-signal combinations, customer segments, conditional exceptions, and rule sequencing.

Before the redesign, the configuration model expressed simple rules. Analysts could represent part of their strategy, but conditional logic across multiple signals, exception handling for customer segments, and policy sequencing required engineering intervention. The interface could not carry the full structure of the analysts' fraud strategy.

Creative Navy-recorded design work used Sandbox Experiments to document the strategies analysts needed to express. The work mapped fraud scenarios, the conditions that separated good detection from false positives, and the exception logic needed to reduce friction for legitimate customers. This made good policy configuration explicit as a design requirement.

Concept Convergence produced an interaction architecture that treated policies as coherent units bundling conditions, actions, history, and audit trail. The three-gesture interaction model represented conditional logic, exception handling, and sequencing that the earlier simple-rule interface could not represent. An evaluation mode let analysts test configurations against simulated transaction contexts and observe whether the policy behaved as intended.

bodySections.heading: Puraite: AI Suggestion Criteria Were Made Visible at the Decision Point
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the documented Puraite case, the AI-assisted systematic review tool made inclusion and exclusion decisions that reviewers needed to evaluate. Experienced systematic reviewers knew that a trustworthy AI decision should be grounded in the specific publication text, applied to criteria that implement the approved protocol, and expressed at a confidence level that reflects the evidence behind it.

At the start of the engagement, what the AI should surface at the decision point was not specified as a design requirement. The interface showed AI decisions without showing enough of the evaluative standard. Less experienced reviewers could not reliably judge whether to accept or override the AI suggestion because the basis for evaluation was not present in the interface.

Creative Navy's design work used four iterations of the AI suggestion display to convert implicit evaluation knowledge into an explicit specification. The first theory showed the decision and criteria, but the criteria were disconnected from the specific evidence that supported them. The second theory added an expandable evidence panel, but the added interaction cost accumulated across hundreds of decisions. The third theory used a compact evidence summary, but compression removed precision needed for substantive override decisions.

The fourth theory became the explicit specification: the decision, criteria, and direct quote from the publication were visible in the side panel from the outset, without additional interaction. This made the AI's behaviour evaluable by experienced reviewers and by less experienced users who could read the evidence and criteria together.

bodySections.heading: KISPE Space and Schone Airspace Group Show Explicit Behaviour Definition Outside AI Products
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
KISPE Space and Schone Airspace Group demonstrate that explicit behaviour definition is not only an AI issue. Both examples concern systems without a model, inference, or recommendations. Their behavioural specifications govern sources, links, protocols, clocks, availability, and interface state rather than AI outputs.

In the KISPE Space case, Creative Navy-recorded design work specified 61 behavioural rules in ten families: geographic and workspace context, time, imagery, satellite services, provenance and uncertainty, notifications, connectivity, briefings, integration and diagnostics, and field presentation. Each rule carried a trigger, a required response, a guard describing what the behaviour must not do, and a specific verification check.

The KISPE Space relevance to this failure is that tacit expectations were converted into explicit, checkable design requirements before build. The verification vocabulary must be read as specification rather than executed testing. The product was built, but Creative Navy did not support the build and has not compared the built interface against the delivered designs.

In the Schone Airspace Group case, Creative Navy-recorded design work specified 12 principal interaction contracts. Each contract defined the initiating action, state transition, visible result, required source inputs, exception behaviour, and check conditions. The design work also stated eight operational invariants as the binding acceptance core of the interaction specification.

The Schone Airspace Group technical register included eight non-negotiable interface rules from the integration side. These separated requested, acknowledged, and observed command facts; kept aircraft focus separate from command target; kept interface target selection separate from flight controller authority; scoped telemetry freshness to source aircraft and fields; separated alert acknowledgement from condition resolution; prevented recorded data appearing as live data; kept stream availability separate from control link health; and prevented unsupported capabilities being represented as operational. The product was built and is in test, not deployed or in operational use.

bodySections.heading: How Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design Method Addresses This Failure
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

For this failure, Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses the implicit-to-explicit conversion through domain learning and iterative testing. Domain learning establishes what good behaviour means in operational terms. Iterative testing discovers the design form through which that knowledge becomes explicit in the interface.

In the Callsign engagement, domain learning mapped the fraud scenarios analysts needed to cover, the conditions they needed to express, and the places where existing configurations failed to represent analyst intent. That mapping converted implicit knowledge of good policy configuration into explicit interaction-architecture requirements.

In the Puraite engagement, domain learning used a methodological adaptation: a team member's firsthand experience with systematic review software served as the domain learning proxy because the timeline did not permit direct user research. This tradeoff was presented to the client explicitly. The four iterations of the AI suggestion display were then evaluated against domain-grounded criteria rather than aesthetic preference.

The iteration described in these examples is not iteration on visual design alone. It is progressive specification of product behaviour: candidate designs reveal what the behaviour specification must include, which failure modes remain, and what information or control must be visible at the point of use.

strongClaims: Good behaviour is not defined explicitly when a team can describe good product behaviour but has not converted that knowledge into an explicit design requirement embodied by the interface.
This failure differs from a product with no clear behaviour model because the behaviour model exists as tacit knowledge rather than being absent altogether.
One expression of the failure is an interface that cannot represent the full reasoning domain experts bring to the work.
A second expression is an AI-assisted interface that surfaces AI outputs without surfacing the criteria users need to evaluate those outputs.
In the Callsign case, the pre-redesign configuration model could express simple rules but not the full conditional logic, exception handling, and sequencing that fraud analysts needed.

In the Puraite case, four iterations of the AI suggestion display converted implicit systematic-review evaluation knowledge into a specification showing the decision, criteria, and direct publication quote without additional interaction.
KISPE Space specified 61 behavioural rules in ten families, each with a trigger, required response, guard, and verification check, to make tacit expectations explicit before build.

Schone Airspace Group specified 12 principal interaction contracts, eight operational invariants, and eight non-negotiable interface rules, with the product built and in test rather than deployed or operational.
weakerClaims: The Callsign case reports Lloyds Bank and HSBC contracts following demos with the redesigned policy engine as a client-reported commercial outcome.
The Puraite outcome evidence is limited to a client-reported shift from theoretical to active use and a single user quote relayed through the client, with no measured task-time or error-rate data.
limitations: The Callsign commercial outcome is client-reported and should not be treated as independently measured product-performance evidence.
The Puraite outcome evidence is client-reported and indirect; no measured task-time or error-rate data is available in the source material.
KISPE Space verification checks are specifications of checks, not executed verification; Creative Navy did not support the build or compare the built interface against the delivered designs.
KISPE Space and Schone Airspace Group should not be framed as AI examples because neither product has a model, performs inference, or makes recommendations.

Schone Airspace Group evidence supports specified contracts, invariants, rules, and test status only; it does not support deployment, operational-use, flight-safety, airworthiness, certification, or measured outcome claims.
The examples are case-specific and do not establish that explicit behaviour specification guarantees commercial, operational, or adoption outcomes.
